doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Albums as wholes and how he built a set
summary: He disclaims a concept but describes opening with instrumentals then vocals.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: They used to have a studio on West 58th Street. Your presentation is similar... Even your first album, Back Country Suite, is conceived of as an album. Did you think about recordings that way, as a complete album that was telling a particular story?
Well, I started Prestige with Back Country Suite. But I made later Transfiguration of Hiram Brown on Columbia...
But they were kind of grouped like an entirety...like the album was one work with sub... I think that’s what he’s asking. Did you conceive them as a whole, like the album was all parts of one whole?
I remember that you had an idea of how every album should balance out, because of...
Well, I remember your saying to an interviewer... He said, “Did Young Man

Mose and Young Man Blues...was that like bookends?” You said, “No.” Then he asked you if you had...something about what reason you had for writing it, and you said, “Well, I figured I needed a blues, and so I wrote it.” It was just a simple thing like that. I know when you put sets together, you always have something in mind that you...
He doesn’t share those thoughts with us.

I think most artists when they’re putting together the set, they want a blues, they want a ballad, they want a burner, they want something mid-tempo. But there’s also a narrative quality to what you do because you’re also writing...
I used to play a couple of instrumentals, and start out a set that way. Then I came on the vocals, and I finished the set that way.

As a writer, maybe there are just these threads going on that you intuit, and you’re not conscious of them, and when you’re done with the product, it somehow coheres. But the reason I’m asking is because, again, I’m interested in why pop artists, musicians who aren’t improvisers but who are singer-songwriters or more commercial music, were attracted to what you did. And that’s a concept you see much more commonly on pop records than you do on jazz records, which tend to be more abstract. So you probably connected deeply with people who heard your lyrics...
What are you asking, by the way.
I’m just making an observation, that’s all.
He’s just making an observation, how all these young singer-songwriters, more commercial artists were attracted to your material.
